intro: Purchasing managers negotiate, manage people and control costs, skills that sales and marketing leadership share. The closest of the 25 careers below is Sales Managers, with an 89% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $148,270, about the same as the $148,080 purchasing managers earn.
why_it_works: Running procurement means choosing suppliers, negotiating contracts and keeping a team on schedule while costs stay down. O*NET rates managing people at 4 out of 5 for this job, and social perceptiveness, time management and negotiation at 3.88. Sales, marketing and compliance leadership use the same skills. Because pay is already high, only 3 matches pay more. The gaps are systems evaluation and operations.
tips: Sales management is the mirror image of your job: same pay, but on the selling side.
Marketing Managers earn $166,790, which is 13% more, and are an 86% match.
Loss prevention and compliance management are 79–80% matches with medians of $141,900.

faq.q: What jobs can former purchasing managers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Sales Managers (89%), Marketing Managers (86%) and Compliance Managers (80%), based on O*NET 31.0. Loss Prevention Managers are 79% matched, with a median of $141,900 for their broader group, and use your supplier and risk knowledge.

faq.q: Which careers for purchasing managers pay more?
faq.a: Only 3 of the 25 matches pay more than $148,080. Chief Executives earn $213,990 (45% more), architectural and engineering managers $171,270 (16% more) and Marketing Managers $166,790 (13% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. The first two usually need a graduate degree.

faq.q: Do purchasing managers need another degree?
faq.a: Usually not. 22 of the 25 matches need no more education than purchasing managers already have, including 9 of the top 10, while 3 need a graduate degree. A bachelor's degree is common, held by 71% of workers in the closest match.

faq.q: What skills should purchasing managers learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are systems evaluation, operation and control, complex problem solving and operations analysis. Negotiation already rates 3.88 out of 5 for this job in O*NET, so analyzing operations is the main step toward executive roles.
